questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following:

(i) Budget surplus. (2 marks)
(ii) Debt servicing. (2 marks)
(iii) Tax base. (2 marks)
(iv) Regressive tax. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Budget surplus.** A budget surplus occurs when the government's **total revenue is greater than its total expenditure** in a financial year. The surplus can be used to repay debt or be kept as a reserve.

**(ii) Debt servicing.** Debt servicing is the **payment of interest and the repayment of the capital (principal)** on the loans of the government, as they fall due. It is a charge on the budget each year.

**(iii) Tax base.** The tax base is the **item (income, profit, wealth, spending or goods) on which a tax is levied**, and so the total value that can be taxed. For example, the tax base of income tax is income, of value added tax (VAT) is the value added on goods and services sold, and of import duty is the value of imported goods. A wider tax base allows the government to collect more revenue.

**(iv) Regressive tax.** A regressive tax **takes a larger proportion of the income of the poor than of the rich**: the tax rate falls as income rises. Example (hypothetical): a fixed charge of 10,000 FCFA is paid by two people; one earns 50,000 FCFA per month and the other 200,000 FCFA. The first pays $\frac{10\,000}{50\,000}\times100=20\%$ of income and the second only $\frac{10\,000}{200\,000}\times100=5\%$. Taxes on basic necessities such as salt or kerosene have the same effect.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Distinguish between the following concepts:

(i) Tax impact and tax incidence. (4 marks)
(ii) Dead weight debt and reproductive debt. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Tax impact and tax incidence.**

- **Tax impact** is the **point at which the tax is first levied**: it falls on the person or firm that is legally responsible for paying the tax to the government (for example the manufacturer who must pay the tax on a drink to the tax office).
- **Tax incidence** is the **final resting place of the burden of the tax**: it falls on the person who actually bears the cost after the tax has been shifted (for example the consumer, if the manufacturer raises the price to recover the tax).

The two may be the same person (income tax paid by the worker, who cannot shift it) or different persons (a tax on goods, shifted forward to buyers in the price or backward to suppliers). Incidence depends largely on the elasticity of demand and supply.

**(ii) Dead weight debt and reproductive debt.**

- **Dead weight debt** is a government debt **used for unproductive purposes** (war, salaries, subsidies, consumption spending) which creates no asset or income to help repay it. The interest and the capital have to be paid out of taxation, so it is a burden on taxpayers.
- **Reproductive debt** (productive debt) is a debt **used to finance productive projects** (roads, dams, power stations, ports, factories) which raise output and create income or tax revenue, so that the project helps to pay back the debt. It does not impose a net burden on the future.

questions.enonce_markdown: State and explain TWO (2) effects of taxation to the economy. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Taxation is the compulsory payment of money to the government without any direct return. Its main effects on the economy are as follows.

1. **It reduces inequality by redistributing income.** With progressive taxes (the rich pay a higher percentage), the government takes more from high earners and spends on schools, hospitals and social services which benefit everybody, especially the poor. The gap between rich and poor narrows and the standard of living of low-income groups rises.
2. **It affects work, saving, investment and the pattern of spending.** Very high taxes on income or profits can discourage people from working harder and firms from investing (a disincentive effect), whereas lower taxes encourage effort and investment. The government can also use taxes to discourage consumption of harmful goods (tobacco and alcohol) and to protect local industry (import duties), and so change what is produced and consumed.

**Conclusion.** Taxes also finance public goods and infrastructure, but they have to be fixed at a level that does not destroy the incentive to work and invest.
